newsitem.title: GERMANY: Soldiers save east German dike before Kohl visit.
newsitem.headline: Soldiers save east German dike before Kohl visit.

text.p: Hundreds of soldiers, assisted by helicopters, staged a spectacular overnight operation to prevent the total collapse of a dike in flood-hit eastern Germany, officials said on Tuesday.

A team of 700 soldiers and relief workers battled through the night to shore up a six to seven metre (yard) section of the dike, which had collapsed and nearly caused a total break in the dam on the Oder River near the village of Hohenwutzen.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl was scheduled to interrupt his summer holiday later on Tuesday to visit the region, where officials said the situation remained critical.
Matthias Platzeck, the environment minister for Brandenburg, the German state worst affected by the floods, said he was considering shoring up more of the dike at Hohenwutzen.
"That appears to be the most vulnerable section, although exact predictions after 12 or 13 days of continuous (water) pressure are no longer possible," he said.
"We've had the greatest pressure on these dikes for all this time and it's pressure which is far above what they were designed for," Platzeck told ZDF television.

The floods have claimed more than 100 lives in neighbouring Poland and the Czech Republic. Germany has so far escaped the worst of the damage, but thousands of residents have already been evacuated from their homes and thousands more are on standby to leave at a moment's notice if the dikes give way.

Officials said up to nine helicopters had flown non-stop during the overnight operation, which was continuing by day. Around 100,000 sandbags had been used to plug the gap and another 100,000 had been ordered, Platzeck said.
Further south, where the Oder and Neisse rivers meet, relief workers had begun building up an 800-metre secondary dike, anticipating a possible break in the main dam near the town of Ratzdorf.
Brandenburg officials said a new wave of high water was approaching Ratzdorf and would reach the most critical areas of the east German stretch of the Oder by afternoon.
Platzeck said the operation to construct a second line of defence by raising up old dikes was a precaution and he was hopeful they would limit flooding if the first dike bursts.
"The condition (of the old dikes) is relatively good, although they haven't been used for decades, or even centuries in some cases," he said.
"Nevertheless, we want to do the maximum to hold the first line of defence because there's a lot of places in front of the secondary dikes and they should stay as dry as possible."
